When the vote doesn’t count: Calif. voters rejected Madera Co.’s newest casino. Inside the furious legal battle unfolding before it opens.

byDaniel Gligich
September 28, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:40
Instaread

A new casino in Madera County is slated to open in October, but not without more than its fair share of buzz – both in marketing and legal fights.

The North Fork Mono Casino and Resort, located just north of Madera fronting Highway 99, is scheduled to open despite being rejected by California voters for off-reservation gaming and a slew of lawsuits from its neighbors,

Decades in the making: The North Fork Rancheria of Mono Indians, whose reservation sits in the Sierra Nevada foothills of Madera County, began planning its casino in 2003, kicking off the federal review process that took until 2011. 

  • Former Gov. Jerry Brown approved the plan to open a gambling facility far away from ancestral lands with a gaming compact in 2012, which received the green light from the California Legislature the following year. 
  • But California voters rejected the compact in 2014 by opposing Proposition 48, shooting down Brown’s decision that the tribe could build a casino along Highway 99. 
  • The U.S. Department of the Interior went on to approve a federal gaming compact with the tribe in 2016. 

Lawsuits come into play: Following Proposition 48, Chukchansi filed a lawsuit claiming that the gaming compact negotiated with Brown was void. A Madera County Superior Court judge ultimately sided with Chukchansi in 2024. 

  • North Fork appealed that ruling but was hit with another rejection from an appellate court, which found that voters exercised their power to shoot down the state gaming compact and that Brown’s approval was void from the moment he issued it.
  • North Fork also appealed that ruling, but the California Supreme Court declined to review it, leaving the appellate court’s decision in place. 
  • Along with the state lawsuits, North Fork has faced multiple federal lawsuits from Chukchansi that have been unsuccessful in halting the project. 

North Fork continues on: Despite not having state approval, the tribe has moved forward with constructing the casino just north of Madera off of Highway 99, saying that it only needs the green light from the federal government to do so. 

  • North Fork broke ground on the casino in September 2024 and has announced that the casino will open in the coming weeks. 
  • The property will span 260,000 square feet and have more than 2,400 slot machines, 40 table games, a 200-room hotel at a later date, parking for RVs and buses and will employ more than 1,500 people. The project is expected to cost $725 million in total. 

11th hour lawsuit from Chukchansi: Chukchansi is trying once again to block the casino before it opens, filing a federal lawsuit in June against North Fork. 

  • Federal law requires that land acquired by Federally-recognized Native American tribes after 1988 must pass a two-part determination by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior: that the casino will be in the best interest of the Indian tribe and its members, and that it will not be detrimental to the surrounding community.
  • Even if those two determinations are met, it must be agreed upon – or concurred – by the Governor of the state where the casino is slated to open.
  • Chukchansi argues that the 2024 ruling by California’s Superior Court and Court of Appeal, which found that North Fork’s gaming compact is void by virtue of the rejection of Prop. 48, means that there is no valid concurrence from the State of California and gaming at the off-reservation resort would be illegal.
  • North Fork has moved to dismiss the lawsuit and is set to open unless a federal judge steps in with a temporary restraining order.

Bernie Sanders returns to the Valley this weekend, eyeing to aid Randy Villegas against Valadao

The progressive duo will appear together in Bakersfield on Sunday.
byDaniel Gligich
September 28, 2026

Socialist Senator Bernie Sanders is heading to Bakersfield this weekend to campaign for the billionaire tax on the November ballot. 

He will be joined by Visalia Unified School District Trustee Randy Villegas, who is running for Congress against Rep. David Valadao (R–Hanford). 

What we’re watching: Sanders announced Monday that he is returning to California for his Fighting Oligarchy Tour. 

  • He will kick off the California swing in San Francisco on Saturday, appearing alongside Rep. Ro Khanna (D–Fremont) and California Insurance Commissioner candidate Jane Kim. 
  • Sanders will continue his tour in Bakersfield on Sunday alongside Villegas, who he has endorsed for Congress. The event will take place at Bakersfield High School at 6 p.m. 
  • Next Monday, Sanders will reunite with Khanna and Kim in Los Angeles to continue his push for the billionaire tax. 

What he’s saying: “At a time when the billionaire class wields enormous power over our economy and political system, join me in California to demand that billionaires finally pay their fair share and help elect strong progressives to Congress,” Sanders said on X. 

Flashback: Villegas joined Khanna for the Congressman’s town hall series in March of last year, where he hinted at his upcoming run against Valadao before ultimately launching his campaign the next month. 

  • Sanders previously appeared in Bakersfield as part of his Fighting Oligarchy tour in April 2025. He was joined by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the time, and they spent much of the event going after Valadao. 
  • After the previous Bakersfield rally, Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez were caught boarding a $15,000 per hour luxury private jet to continue their tour.

Fresno Metropolitan Flood Control District to open field trip grant program

Students in the Fresno area could visit Scout Island along the San Joaquin River as part of the program.
byDaniel Gligich
September 28, 2026

The Fresno Metropolitan Flood Control District is opening applications to its grant program this week that provides funding for local schools to take field trips. 

Along with opening up applications to the long-standing grant program, the Flood Control District announced that it is making it easier for schools to use in light of the recent field trip funding controversy at Fresno Unified School District. 

The big picture: The 2027 Clean Stormwater Grant Program will offer up to $40,000 in funding for local schools, nonprofits and community organizations to support environmental education, water-resource field trips and projects that protect local waterways. 

  • Water Resources Field Trip Grants are up to $2,000 per grant, while General Grants are up to $4,000. 

Changes for this year: While the grant program was established in 1997, the Flood Control District is paying field trip and transportation vendors directly this year. Previously, school districts had to pay field trip expenses upfront before getting reimbursed. 

  • Schools will also have expanded flexibility for Scout Island field trips. They will be able to select from the full range of learning activities offered, as long as at least two are water-resource-based and the costs remain within the $2,000 grant award. 

Driving the news: The Flood Control District said the changes were implemented because of recent concerns over Fresno Unified field trip funding. 

  • Fresno Unified cut funding for all elementary schools this year, totaling a $2.2 million budget cut. After significant public outcry, the district announced that the Foundation for Fresno Unified Students has stepped up to cover all field trip costs this year. 

What we’re watching: Applications for the grant program will open on Thursday and be accepted through Dec. 18. 

What they’re saying: “We want to make it easier for local schools and organizations to turn good ideas into meaningful opportunities for our community,” said Assistant General Manager Berta Mims. “Whether that means giving students a hands-on experience with local water resources or supporting a project that helps protect those resources, these grants are an investment in education, stewardship and the future of our region.”
